pairs.en: **Matthew 18:21.**

*"Then Peter came to Him and said, Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times? Jesus says to him, I do not say to you, Until seven times, but, Until seventy times seven."* [Matthew 18:21-22]

Peter supposed he was saying something great; that is why, aiming at greatness, he added, *"Until seven times?"* For what You have commanded us to do, he means — how often shall I do it? If a man keeps on sinning, and keeps on repenting whenever he is reproved, how often do You command us to bear with him? With regard to the other man, the one who does not repent and will not acknowledge his own faults, You have set a limit, saying, *"Let him be to you as the Gentile and the tax collector"* [Matthew 18:17]. But for this one You have not done so; You have commanded us to accept him.
How often, then, ought I to bear with him, when he is told his faults and repents? Is seven times enough?

What then does Christ say — the good God, who is loving toward mankind? *"I do not say to you, until seven times, but until seventy times seven"* — not setting a number here, but what is infinite and perpetual and forever. For just as "ten thousand times" means "often," so it is here as well. When Scripture says, *"The barren has borne seven,"* [1 Samuel 2:5] it means many. So He has not limited forgiveness by a number; He has declared that it is to be perpetual and forever.

This at least He indicated by the parable that follows. For that He might not seem to anyone to be enjoining great things and hard to bear by saying *"Seventy times seven,"* He added this parable — at once leading them on to what He had said, putting down the man who was priding himself on this, and showing that the act was not grievous, but rather very easy. And let me add: He brought forward His own love toward mankind, so that by the comparison, as He says, you might learn that though you forgive seventy times seven, though you continually pardon your neighbor for absolutely all his sins, still, as a drop of water beside an endless sea — so much, or rather far more, does your love toward mankind fall short of the boundless goodness of God, of which you stand in need, because you are to be judged and to give an account.

sections.heading: Ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii

pairs.en: That is why He went on to say: *"The Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. And when he had begun to reckon, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents. But since he had nothing to pay, he commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and his children, and all that he had."* [Matthew 18:23-25]

Then, after this man had enjoyed the benefit of mercy, he went out and seized his fellow-servant by the throat — the one who owed him a hundred denarii [Matthew 18:28] — and by these doings he moved his lord, and caused him to cast him again into prison until he should pay off the whole.

Do you see how great the difference is between sins against man and sins against God? As great as between ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii — or rather, even much more. And this arises both from the difference of the persons, and from the constant succession of our sins. For when a man looks at us, we stand off and shrink from sinning; but when God sees us every day, we do not hold back, but do and speak all things without fear.
And not from this alone, but also from the benefit and from the honor of which we have partaken, our sins become more grievous.

sections.heading: How our sins are ten thousand talents

pairs.en: And if you wish to learn how our sins against Him are ten thousand talents — or rather even much more — I will try to show it briefly. But I fear lest, to those who are inclined to wickedness and love to go on sinning, I should furnish still greater security, or should drive the meeker sort to despair, and they should repeat that saying of the disciples, *"Who then can be saved?"* [Matthew 19:25]

Nevertheless, for all that I will speak, that I may make those who attend more safe, and more meek. For they who are incurably diseased and past feeling do not leave off their own carelessness and wickedness even without these words of mine; and if even from this they take a greater occasion for contempt, the fault is not in what is said, but in their insensibility. What is said is surely enough both to restrain those who attend to it and to prick their hearts. And the meeker sort, when they see on the one hand the greatness of their sins, and learn on the other the power of repentance, will cleave to it the more. Therefore it is needful to speak.

I will speak then, and will set forth our sins, both those in which we offend against God and those in which we offend against men. I will set forth not each person's own, but what are common; and after that let each one join his own to them from his conscience.

And I will do this after first setting forth the good deeds of God toward us. What then are His good deeds? He created us when we were not, and made all things that are seen for our sakes — heaven, sea, air, all that is in them, living creatures, plants, seeds — for we must speak briefly, because of the boundless ocean of the works. Into us alone of all that are on earth He breathed a living soul such as we have. He planted a garden. He gave a helpmeet. He set us over all the brute beasts. He crowned us with glory and honor.
After that, when man had been unthankful toward his Benefactor, He granted him a still greater gift.

sections.heading: Cast out of paradise, and given still more

pairs.en: For do not look only at this, that He cast him out of paradise; mark also the gain that arose from it. For after having cast him out of paradise, and having worked those countless good works, and having accomplished His various dispensations, He sent even His own Son for the sake of those who had been benefited by Him and were hating Him. He opened heaven to us, and unfolded paradise itself, and made us sons — us, the enemies, the unthankful.
So it would be seasonable now to say, *"O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!"* [Romans 11:33]

And He gave us also a baptism of the remission of sins, and a deliverance from vengeance, and an inheritance of a kingdom. He promised numberless good things if we do what is right, and stretched forth His hand, and poured out His Spirit into our hearts.

What then? After so many and such great blessings, what ought our disposition to be? Even if each day we died for Him who so loves us, should we make due recompense — or rather, should we repay even the smallest portion of the debt? By no means. For even this again is turned to our advantage.

How then are we disposed, we whose disposition ought to be like this? Each day we insult His law. But do not be angry if I let loose my tongue against those who sin, for I will not accuse you only, but myself also.

Where then would you have me begin? With the slaves, or with the free? With those who serve in the army, or with private persons? With the rulers, or with the subjects? With the women, or with the men? With the aged, or with the young? With what age? With what race? With what rank? With what pursuit?

sections.heading: The sins of those who serve as soldiers

pairs.en: Would you have me begin with those who serve as soldiers? What sin, then, do these not commit every day — insulting, reviling, frantic, making a gain of other men's calamities, being like wolves, never clear of offenses, unless one were to say that the sea too is without waves? What passion does not trouble them? What disease does not lay siege to their soul?

Toward their equals they show a jealous disposition; they envy, and they hunt after vainglory. Toward those subject to them their disposition is covetous. But toward those who have lawsuits and run to them as to a harbor, their conduct is that of enemies and perjured persons. How many robberies are there among them! How many frauds! How many false accusations, and meannesses! How many servile flatteries!

Come then, let us apply in each case the law of Christ. *"He who says to his brother, You fool, shall be in danger of hell fire."* [Matthew 5:22] *"He who has looked on a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her."* [Matthew 5:28] Unless one humbles himself as the little child, he shall not enter into the Kingdom of Heaven. [Matthew 18:3-4]

But these even study haughtiness. Toward those who are subject to them, and are delivered into their hands, and who tremble at them and are afraid of them, they become fiercer than a wild beast — doing nothing for Christ's sake, but all things for the belly, for money, for vainglory.

Can one even reckon up in words the trespass of their actions? What should one say of their decisions, their laughter, their unseasonable discourses, their filthy language? But about covetousness one cannot so much as speak. For just as the monks on the mountains do not even know what covetousness is, so neither do these — but in the opposite way. Those, because they are far removed from the disease, do not know the passion; these, because they are exceedingly intoxicated with it, have not so much as a perception of how great the evil is. For this vice has so thrust virtue aside and tyrannizes, that among those madmen it is not even accounted a heavy charge.

sections.heading: Workmen, artisans, and those who hold land

pairs.en: But would you have us leave these, and go to others of a gentler kind? Come then, let us examine the race of workmen and artisans. For these above all seem to live by honest labors and the sweat of their own brow. But these too, when they do not take heed to themselves, gather to themselves many evils from this very thing. For the dishonesty that arises from buying and selling they bring into the work of honest labor, and they often add oaths and perjuries and falsehoods to their covetousness. They are taken up with worldly things only, and remain riveted to the earth; and while they do all things that they may get money, they do not take much heed that they may impart to the needy, being always desirous to increase their goods. What should one say of the revilings that are uttered in such matters, the insults, the loans, the usurious gains, the bargains full of much mean trafficking, the shameless buyings and sellings?

But would you have us leave these too, and go to others who seem to be more just? Who then are they? Those who possess lands, and reap the wealth that springs from the earth. And what can be more unjust than these? For if anyone were to examine how they treat their wretched and toil-worn laborers, he will see them to be more cruel than savages. For upon those who are pining with hunger and toiling throughout all their life they impose constant and intolerable payments, and they lay on them laborious burdens, and they treat their bodies like asses or mules — or rather like stones — allowing them not so much as to draw breath a little. And when the earth yields, and when it does not yield, they alike wear them out, and grant them no indulgence. And what can be more pitiable than this: when, after having labored throughout the whole winter, and being consumed with frost and rain and watchings, they go away with their hands empty — yes, and moreover in debt — fearing and dreading more than this famine and shipwreck the torments of the overseers, and their dragging them about, and their demands, and their imprisonments, and the services from which no entreaty can deliver them?

Why should one speak of the merchandise they make of them, the sordid gains they get by them — by their labors and their sweat filling winepresses and wine-vats, yet not suffering them to take home so much as a small measure, but draining off the entire fruits into the casks of their wickedness, and flinging to them for this a little money?

They devise new kinds of usury as well, not lawful even according to the laws of the heathen, and they frame contracts for loans full of many a curse. For they press for and exact not the hundredth part of the sum, but the half of the sum — and this when he of whom it is exacted has a wife, is bringing up children, is a human being, and is filling their threshing-floor and their winepress by his own toils.

But none of these things do they consider. So now it would be seasonable to bring forward the prophet and say, *"Be astonished, O heaven, and be horribly afraid, O earth,"* [Jeremiah 2:12] to what great brutality the race of man has been madly carried away!

But I say these things not blaming crafts, nor husbandry, nor military service, but ourselves. For Cornelius also was a centurion, and Paul a worker in leather, and after his preaching still practiced his craft, and David was a king, and Job enjoyed the possession of land and of large revenues, and there was no hindrance from any of this in the way of virtue.

Bearing in mind all these things, and considering the ten thousand talents, let us at least from this hasten to remit to our neighbors their few and trifling debts. For we too have an account to give of the commandments with which we have been trusted, and we are not able to pay all, no matter what we may do. Therefore God has given us a way of repayment both ready and easy, and able to cancel all these things — I mean, not to be revengeful.

In order then that we may learn this well, let us hear the whole parable, going through it in order. For there was brought to Him, it says, one who owed ten thousand talents, and when he had not the means to pay, He commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and his children. Why, I ask you? Not from cruelty, nor from inhumanity — for the loss came back again upon Himself, since she too was a slave — but from unspeakable tenderness.

For it is His purpose to alarm him by this threat, that He might bring him to supplication, not that he should be sold. For if He had done it with that intent, He would not have consented to his request, nor would He have granted the favor.

Why then did He not do this, nor forgive the debt before the account? Because He desired to teach him from how many obligations He was delivering him, so that in this way at least he might become more mild toward his fellow-servant. For if, even when he had learned the weight of his debt and the greatness of the forgiveness, he went on taking his fellow-servant by the throat — if He had not disciplined him beforehand with such medicines, to what length of cruelty might he not have gone?
What then does the other say? *"Have patience with me, and I will pay you all." And his lord was moved with compassion, and released him, and forgave him the debt.* [Matthew 18:26-27]

Do you see again a surpassing benevolence? The servant asked only for delay and a putting-off of the time, but He gave more than he asked: remission and forgiveness of the entire debt. For it had been His will to give it even from the first, but He did not desire the gift to be His only, but also to come of this man's entreaty, so that he might not go away uncrowned. That the whole was from Him, even though this other fell down and prayed, the motive of the forgiveness showed: for moved with compassion, He forgave him. But still, even so, He willed that the other also should seem to contribute something, so that he might not be exceedingly covered with shame, and so that he, schooled by his own calamities, might be indulgent to his fellow-servant.

sections.heading: Fresh from mercy, he takes his fellow-servant by the throat

pairs.en: Up to this point, then, this man was good and acceptable: for he confessed, and promised to pay the debt, and fell down before him, and entreated, and condemned his own sins, and knew the greatness of the debt. But the sequel is unworthy of his former deeds. For going out straightway — not after a long time, but straightway, having the benefit still fresh upon him — he abused to wickedness the gift, even the freedom bestowed on him by his master.
For *"he found one of his fellow-servants who owed him a hundred denarii, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me what you owe."* [Matthew 18:28]
Do you see the master's benevolence? Do you see the servant's cruelty? Hear this, you who do these things for money. For if we must not do so for sins, much more must we not do so for money.

What then does the other say? *"Have patience with me, and I will pay you all."* But he did not regard even the words by which he himself had been saved — for he himself, on saying this, was delivered from the ten thousand talents — and he did not recognize so much as the harbor by which he escaped shipwreck. The gesture of supplication did not remind him of his master's kindness, but he put away from him all these things, from covetousness and cruelty and revenge, and was more fierce than any wild beast, seizing his fellow-servant by the throat.

What are you doing, O man? Do you not perceive that you are making the demand upon yourself, that you are thrusting the sword into yourself, and revoking the sentence and the gift? But none of these things did he consider, neither did he remember his own state, neither did he yield — although the entreaty was not even for equal objects.

For the one had besought for ten thousand talents, the other for a hundred denarii; the one his fellow-servant, the other his lord; the one received entire forgiveness, the other asked for delay — and not even this did he give him, for he cast him into prison.
But when his fellow-servants saw it, they accused him to their lord. Not even to men is this well-pleasing, much less to God. They therefore who did not owe, partook of the grief.
What then does their lord say? *"O you wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt, because you asked me; should you not also have had compassion, even as I had pity on you?"* [Matthew 18:32-33]

See again the lord's gentleness. He pleads with him, and excuses himself, being on the point of revoking his gift; or rather, it was not he that revoked it, but the one who had received it. That is why He says, *"I forgave you all that debt, because you asked me; should you not also have had compassion on your fellow-servant?"* For even if the thing does seem hard to you, yet you should have looked to the gain — which has been, which is to be. Even if the injunction is galling, you ought to consider the reward; and not that he has grieved you, but that you have provoked God, whom by mere prayer you have reconciled. But if even so it is a galling thing to you to become friends with him who has grieved you, to fall into hell is far more grievous; and if you had set this against that, then you would have known that to forgive is a much lighter thing.

And whereas, when he owed ten thousand talents, he called him not wicked, nor reproached him, but showed mercy on him — when he had become harsh to his fellow-servant, then he says, *"O you wicked servant."*

Let us listen — we the covetous — for the word is spoken even to us. Let us listen also, we the merciless and the cruel, for we are not cruel to others, but to ourselves. When then you are minded to be revengeful, consider that you are revengeful against yourself, not against another; that you are binding up your own sins, not your neighbor's. For as to you, whatever you may do to this man, you do as a man and in the present life; but God not so — more mightily will He take vengeance on you, and with the vengeance hereafter.

For He delivered him over until he should pay what was due — that is, forever; for he will never repay. For since you have not become better by the kindness shown you, it remains that by vengeance you be corrected.

And yet *"the graces and the gifts are without repentance"* [Romans 11:29] — but wickedness has had such power as to set aside even this law. What then can be a more grievous thing than to be revengeful, when it appears to overthrow such and so great a gift of God?

And he did not merely deliver him, but was angry. For when he commanded him to be sold, those were not the words of wrath (therefore neither did he do it), but a very great occasion for benevolence; but now the sentence is of much indignation, and vengeance, and punishment.
What then does the parable mean? *"So likewise shall My Father do also to you,"* He says, *"if you from your hearts do not forgive every one his brother their trespasses."* [Matthew 18:35]
He says not *"your Father,"* but *"My Father."* For it is not fitting for God to be called the Father of such a one, who is so wicked and malicious.

sections.heading: Condemn yourself, and forgive from the heart

pairs.en: Two things, therefore, does He require here: both to condemn ourselves for our sins, and to forgive others — and the former for the sake of the latter, that this may become more easy (for he who considers his own sins is more indulgent to his fellow-servant); and not merely to forgive with the lips, but from the heart.

Let us not then thrust the sword into ourselves by being revengeful. For what grief has he who has grieved you inflicted upon you, like the grief you will work upon yourself by keeping your anger in mind, and drawing upon yourself the sentence from God that condemns you? For if indeed you are watchful, and keep yourself under control, the evil will come round upon his head, and it will be he that will suffer harm; but if you continue indignant and displeased, then you yourself will undergo the harm — not from him, but from yourself.

Do not say then that he insulted you, and slandered you, and did you ills beyond number; for the more you tell, so much the more do you declare him a benefactor. For he has given you an opportunity to wash away your sins; so that the greater the injuries he has done you, so much more has he become to you a cause of a greater remission of sins.

For if we are willing, no one shall be able to injure us, but even our enemies shall advantage us in the greatest degree. And why do I speak of men? For what can be more wicked than the devil? Yet nevertheless, even from him we have a great opportunity of approving ourselves; and Job shows it. But if the devil has become a cause of crowns, why are you afraid of a man as an enemy?

sections.heading: What we gain by bearing injuries meekly

pairs.en: See then how much you gain, bearing meekly the spiteful acts of your enemies. First and greatest, deliverance from sins; secondly, fortitude and patience; thirdly, mildness and benevolence — for he who does not know how to be angry with those who grieve him will be much more ready to serve those who love him. Fourthly, to be free from anger continually, to which nothing can be equal. For of him who is free from anger it is quite clear that he is delivered also from the despondency that arises from it, and will not spend his life on vain labors and sorrows. For he who does not know how to hate does not know how to grieve either, but will enjoy pleasure, and ten thousand blessings. So that we punish ourselves by hating others, even as, on the other hand, we benefit ourselves by loving them.
Besides all these things, you will be an object of veneration even to your very enemies, though they be demons; or rather, you will not so much as have an enemy while you are of such a disposition.

But what is greater than all, and first: you gain the favor of God. Should you have sinned, you will obtain pardon; should you have done what is right, you will obtain a greater confidence. Let us accomplish therefore the hating of no one, that God also may love us, that, though we be in debt for ten thousand talents, He may have compassion and pity us.

But have you been injured by him? Pity him then; do not hate him. Weep and mourn; do not turn away from him. For you are not the one who has offended against God, but he; and you have even approved yourself, if you endure it. Consider that Christ, when about to be crucified, rejoiced for Himself, but wept for those who were crucifying Him. This ought to be our disposition also; and the more we are injured, so much the more should we lament for those who are injuring us. For to us many are the benefits that arise from this, but to them the opposites.

sections.heading: Insult, slander, and those who forgave

pairs.en: But did he insult you, and strike you before all? Then he has disgraced and dishonored himself before all, and has opened the mouths of a thousand accusers, and for you he has woven more crowns, and gathered for you many to publish your forbearance.

But did he slander you to others? And what is this? God is the one who is to demand the account, not those who have heard it. For to himself he has added occasion of punishment, so that he should give account not only for his own sins, but also for what he said of you. And upon you he has brought evil report with men, but he himself has incurred evil report with God.

And if these things are not sufficient for you, consider that even your Lord was evil spoken of, both by Satan and by men, and that to those most loved by Him; and His Only-Begotten the same again. That is why He said, *"If they have called the Master of the house Beelzebub, how much more shall they call those of His household."* [Matthew 10:25]

And that wicked demon did not only slander Him, but was also believed, and slandered Him not in ordinary matters, but with the greatest reproaches and accusations. For he affirmed Him to be possessed, and to be a deceiver, and an adversary of God.

But have you also done good, and received evil? Nay, in respect of this most of all lament and grieve for him who has done the wrong, but for yourself rather rejoice, because you have become like God, *"who makes His sun to rise upon the evil and the good."* [Matthew 5:45]

But if to follow God is beyond you — although to him who watches, not even this is hard — yet nevertheless, if this seems to you too great for you, come, let us bring you to your fellow-servants: to Joseph, who suffered countless things, and did good to his brethren; to Moses, who after their countless plots against him prayed for them; to the blessed Paul, who cannot so much as number what he suffered from them, and is willing to be accursed for them; to Stephen, who is stoned, and entreats that this sin may be forgiven them. And having considered all these things, cast away all anger, that God may forgive us also all our trespasses, by the grace and love toward mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom to the Father and the Holy Spirit be glory, might, and honor, now and always, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.
